slides.title: AST 101 Week 4: Light
body_text: Light and telescopes
Dr. Alex Morgan
slides.speaker_notes: Almost everything we know about the universe arrived as light.

slides.title: What Is Light?
body_text: An electromagnetic wave
Speed in empty space: about 300,000 km/s
Wavelength x frequency = speed of light
slides.speaker_notes: Short wavelength means high frequency, and the reverse.

slides.title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
body_text: Longest to shortest: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma ray
Visible light: about 700 nm (red) to 400 nm (violet)
Our eyes see only a thin slice
slides.speaker_notes: The piano keyboard: the spectrum is miles of keys and our eyes hear about one octave.

slides.title: Photons
body_text: Light also comes in packets of energy called photons
Shorter wavelength means more energy per photon
That is why ultraviolet can burn skin and radio cannot
slides.speaker_notes: Same light, two descriptions. Both are needed.

slides.title: Thermal Radiation
body_text: Every warm object glows
Hotter objects glow more, at every wavelength
Hotter objects peak at shorter wavelengths: hot is blue, cool is red
The Sun's glow peaks near 500 nm
slides.speaker_notes: A stove burner goes dull red, then orange, then yellow-white as it heats.

slides.title: Atmospheric Windows
body_text: Visible light and most radio waves reach the ground
Water vapor absorbs much of the infrared
Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are blocked
So X-ray and gamma-ray telescopes have to be in space
slides.speaker_notes: The atmosphere protects us and annoys astronomers in equal measure.

slides.title: The Inverse-Square Law
body_text: Light spreads over a sphere whose area grows as distance squared
Brightness goes as 1 / distance squared
Twice as far: one quarter as bright
slides.speaker_notes: Flashlight beam through a square cutout onto a grid at 1 meter and 2 meters: four times the squares.

slides.title: Example: Streetlights
body_text: Two identical streetlights
One is 3 times farther away
It looks 1/9 as bright
slides.speaker_notes: Students invent their own version with a 4 or 5 and swap with a neighbor.

slides.title: What Telescopes Do
body_text: 1. Gather light
2. Resolve fine detail
3. Magnify, the least important job
slides.speaker_notes: Every department-store telescope box advertises magnification. It is the wrong number to look at.

slides.title: Light-Gathering Power
body_text: Proportional to the area of the aperture, so to its diameter squared
Twice the diameter collects four times the light
An 8-meter mirror versus a 7 mm pupil: about 1.3 million times the light
slides.speaker_notes: A telescope is a bucket for light. A wider bucket catches more rain.

slides.title: Resolution
body_text: The smallest angle a telescope can separate shrinks as the aperture grows
Twice the aperture, details twice as fine
A 10 cm telescope resolves about 1 arcsecond in visible light
On the ground, air turbulence blurs most views to about 1 arcsecond
slides.speaker_notes: That blurring is why the sharpest images come from space or from adaptive optics.
